deed: דיוויד בולטימור גילה את אנזים השעתוק ההפוך שפתח דלת למחקר נגיפים וסרטן
title: David Baltimore discovered an enzyme that makes DNA from RNA, and paved the way for drugs against HIV

trailer.text: David Baltimore, an American Jew born in New York in 1938, was one of the laureates of the 1975 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.
According to the Karolinska Institute, the central dogma of molecular biology held at the time that information in nature passes only from DNA to RNA, and not in the other direction.
In 1970 Baltimore, of the Department of Biology at MIT, published a paper in Nature on an enzyme in RNA tumour viruses that synthesizes DNA from an RNA template.
The enzyme was named reverse transcriptase, and the finding was critical to understanding the AIDS virus.
The enzyme became a successful therapeutic target, and as a result several HIV-suppression drugs were developed.

glance.label: Recognition
glance.value: Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine, 1975

stations.title: A Jewish home, a bar mitzvah in Great Neck

paragraphs.text: David Baltimore was born on 7 March 1938 in New York.
His father, Richard Baltimore, was a garment industry merchant, and his mother was Gertrude Lipschitz-Baltimore.
His father's family was an Orthodox Jewish family from Lithuania.
He attended Sunday school at the Conservative synagogue Temple Israel in Great Neck, and had his bar mitzvah there.
According to the Jewish Journal in 2005, he saw himself as a secular Jew whose outlook and achievements are rooted in his early Jewish upbringing.
Baltimore said that his interest in biology began in high school, during a summer at the Jackson Laboratory in Bar Harbor, Maine.
He completed a B.A. in Chemistry with high honors at Swarthmore College in 1960, and received a Ph.D. from Rockefeller University in 1964.
He said that at the Salk Institute in La Jolla, California, he had the opportunity to work in association with Renato Dulbecco.
There he also met his future wife, Alice Shih Huang.
In 1968 he returned to MIT, and remained there until 1990.

stations.title: The rule that information flows only one way

paragraphs.text: According to the Karolinska Institute, Rous had shown more than 60 years earlier that viruses can cause tumours, in studies of sarcomas in chickens.
According to Rockefeller University, Peyton Rous revealed this in 1910.
The central dogma of molecular biology held that information in nature passes only from DNA to RNA, and not in the other direction.
According to the Los Angeles Times, researchers then firmly believed in this rule, and some biologists began to doubt it.

According to Rockefeller University, Howard Temin proposed in the 1960s that an RNA tumour virus might infect healthy cells by making a DNA copy of itself, but the idea was not well received in the scientific community.
According to the Karolinska Institute, most scientists considered this theory heresy, because it contradicted the central dogma.
Baltimore himself had previously studied virus-specific enzymes that copy RNA from RNA.
According to Rockefeller University, in 1970 Temin and Baltimore, each separately, found proof of the theory.
Temin, at the University of Wisconsin, found the proof in avian myeloblastosis virus.
Baltimore worked at MIT with the Rauscher murine leukemia virus and the Rous sarcoma virus.
In his method, Baltimore used nonionic detergents to make the virus membranes permeable and to introduce deoxynucleotides into the particles.
When he detected the synthesis of DNA following the template of the virus's RNA, he effectively proved the theory of reverse transcription.
He published in Nature, volume 226, a paper on RNA-dependent DNA polymerase in RNA tumour viruses, while he belonged to the Department of Biology at MIT.
The abstract stated that two independent groups of investigators had found evidence of an enzyme that synthesizes DNA from an RNA template.
It also stated that apparently the classical process of information transfer from DNA to RNA can be inverted.
That same year, during the experiments that led to the Nobel Prize, Baltimore shut down his lab for a week and joined demonstrators in Boston against the invasion of Cambodia.
According to the Jewish Journal, because of this he almost lost the Nobel Prize, as he shut down the lab on the eve of a breakthrough experiment.
The enzyme was named reverse transcriptase.
A unique family of viruses, the retroviruses, uses it to replicate themselves.
According to NobelPrize.org, the discovery required changing the accepted rule that genetic information passes in only one direction.
According to the Karolinska Institute, since 1970 knowledge of the genetic material of RNA tumour viruses has developed rapidly.
According to Rockefeller University, in the early 1980s reverse transcription was used in identifying HIV as the cause of AIDS.
Reverse transcriptase became a successful therapeutic target for the disease, and as a result several HIV-suppression drugs were developed.
According to Rockefeller University, the isolation of the enzyme, which Baltimore pioneered, is used in recombinant DNA technology.
According to the same source, Baltimore also devised the Baltimore classification system, which divides viruses into seven groups according to genome type.
According to the Los Angeles Times, the discovery was greeted with overheated predictions that science had at last found a cure for cancer.
Baltimore knew that his work did not augur a cure for cancer.
He said that work on the Abelson virus led to the discovery that its oncoprotein is a specific tyrosine kinase, and to the development of the drug Gleevec.
The 1975 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine was awarded jointly to Baltimore, Renato Dulbecco and Howard Temin.
The prize was given for discoveries concerning "the interaction between tumour viruses and the genetic material of the cell".
According to the Karolinska Institute, Dulbecco and coworkers proved that the genetic material of the virus is built into the genetic material of the transformed cells.
According to the Los Angeles Times, Temin discovered the enzyme around the same time as Baltimore.
According to the Karolinska Institute in 1975, it had already been found that both DNA viruses and RNA viruses can cause transformation of cells.
According to the Institute, until then it had not been demonstrated that viruses cause tumours in humans, except for the wart virus.
The Institute wrote that it appeared likely that a link would be found between viruses and the appearance of more serious tumours in humans.
In 1973 Baltimore received a lifetime research professorship from the American Cancer Society, and a year later was elected to the National Academy of Sciences.
At 37, following the prize, he became a recognised savant in the public eye.
In 1999 he received the National Medal of Science, and in 2000 the Warren Alpert Foundation Prize.
According to the Los Angeles Times, he published more than 700 peer-reviewed articles.
Thomas Rosenbaum, then president of Caltech, said that Baltimore's contributions as a virologist transformed biology and medicine.
In the 1970s, Baltimore organized a conference at Asilomar to design a self-regulating system for gene-splicing experiments.
Baltimore was the director of the Whitehead Institute for Biomedical Research from its beginning, but the sources differ on the year and on how he came to the position.
According to Rockefeller University, he assumed the presidency of Rockefeller University in 1990 and returned to MIT in 1994.
According to the same source, in 1997 he accepted the presidency of Caltech and served until 2006.
According to the Los Angeles Times, during his years as president he raised Caltech's profile, and under his leadership the institution raised more than $1.1 billion.
The sources give different numbers for the years of his presidency.
In June 2005 he received a $13.9 million grant from the Grand Challenges in Global Health initiative, supported by the Bill and Melinda Gates Foundation.
David Baltimore died on 6 September 2025 in Woods Hole, Massachusetts.

According to the Whitehead Institute website, in 1982 Baltimore partnered with philanthropist Edwin Jack Whitehead to conceive and launch the institute, and he served as its founding director until 1990.
Baltimore said that he left the presidency of Rockefeller University in 1991 because of a misconduct case involving a collaborator.
According to the Los Angeles Times, his name was attached to the whiff of scandal, even though his own work was never questioned.
According to the same newspaper, after four federal investigations and a grand jury investigation, both Baltimore's colleague and Baltimore himself were exonerated.

claims.text: בשנות ה-70 ארגן בולטימור כנס באסילומר כדי לתכנן מערכת רגולציה עצמית לניסויי שחבור גנים.
claims.quote: Baltimore organized a conference at Asilomar near Monterey to design a self-regulating system to monitor those experiments.

claims.text: לפי אוניברסיטת רוקפלר, בולטימור ייסד ב-1982 את מכון ווייטהד למחקר ביו-רפואי וכיהן כמנהלו.
claims.quote: in 1982 founded the Whitehead Institute for Biomedical Research, which he then served as director

claims.text: לפי הלוס אנג'לס טיימס, ב-1984 נבחר בולטימור למנהל המייסד של מכון ווייטהד.
claims.quote: In 1984, Baltimore was chosen founding director of the new Whitehead Institute for Biomedical Research

claims.text: לפי אוניברסיטת רוקפלר, בולטימור נכנס לנשיאות אוניברסיטת רוקפלר ב-1990 וחזר ל-MIT ב-1994.
claims.quote: He assumed the presidency of Rockefeller University in 1990 and continued as a member of the Rockefeller faculty after his presidential tenure, returning to MIT in 1994.

claims.text: לפי אוניברסיטת רוקפלר, ב-1997 קיבל בולטימור את נשיאות קלטק ושירת עד 2006.
claims.quote: In 1997 he accepted the presidency of the California Institute of Technology, serving until 2006

claims.text: לפי הלוס אנג'לס טיימס, בשמונה שנות נשיאותו העלה בולטימור את פרופיל קלטק.
claims.quote: In his eight years as president, Baltimore raised the university’s profile

claims.text: לפי הלוס אנג'לס טיימס, תחת הנהגתו גייס קלטק יותר מ-1.1 מיליארד דולר.
claims.quote: Under his leadership, Caltech raised more than $1.1 billion.

claims.text: לפי ה-Jewish Journal באוקטובר 2005, בולטימור כיהן תשע שנים כנשיא קלטק.
claims.quote: During his nine-year tenure as Caltech president, the 67-year old Baltimore translated many of his family’s principles into practice

claims.text: ביוני 2005 קיבל בולטימור מענק של 13.9 מיליון דולר ממיזם Grand Challenges in Global Health בתמיכת קרן ביל ומלינדה גייטס.
claims.quote: In June, he received a $13.9 million grant by the Grand Challenges in Global Health initiative, supported by the Bill and Melinda Gates Foundation.

claims.text: דיוויד בולטימור מת ב-6 בספטמבר 2025 בוודס הול, מסצ'וסטס.
claims.quote: Died: 6 September 2025, Woods Hole, MA, USA

claims.text: בולטימור סיפר שעזב את נשיאות רוקפלר ב-1991 בגלל פרשת התנהלות פסולה של משתף פעולה.
claims.quote: I only stayed in that position through 1991 because a misconduct case against a collaborator of mine became a drag on my effectiveness.

claims.text: לפי הלוס אנג'לס טיימס, בולטימור נקשר לחשד לשערורייה אף שעבודתו עצמה מעולם לא הועמדה בספק.
claims.quote: The whiff of scandal was attached to Baltimore himself, even though his work was never questioned.

claims.text: לפי הלוס אנג'לס טיימס, אחרי ארבע חקירות פדרליות וחקירת חבר מושבעים, חברו של בולטימור ובולטימור עצמו נוקו.
claims.quote: Four federal investigations and a grand jury probe later, Baltimore’s colleague, and Baltimore himself, were exonerated.

claims.text: לפי מכון קרולינסקה, ב-1970 הראו טמין ובולטימור בו-זמנית קיום אנזים ספציפי בחלקיקי נגיף RNA סרטני, המסוגל ליצור עותק DNA מ-RNA.
claims.quote: the major breakthrough occurred in 1970 when simultaneously Temin and also David Baltimore showed the occurrence of a specific enzyme in RNA tumour virus particles which could make a DNA copy from RNA

claims.text: לפי אתר מכון ווייטהד, ב-1982 שיתף בולטימור פעולה עם הפילנתרופ אדווין ג'ק ווייטהד כדי להגות ולהשיק את המכון, והוא כיהן כמנהלו המייסד עד 1990.
claims.quote: In 1982, Baltimore partnered with philanthropist Edwin C.

claims.text: מכון קרולינסקה (1975): לפי הדוגמה, מידע עובר בטבע רק מ-DNA ל-RNA ולא בכיוון ההפוך.
claims.quote: This dogma implied that information transfer in nature occurred only from DNA to RNA and not in the other direction.

claims.text: פרנסיס קריק, מנסח הדוגמה (לפי PLOS Biology): הוא מעולם לא טען שמעבר מ-RNA ל-DNA בלתי אפשרי.
claims.quote: rightly insisting that he had never argued that

claims.text: לפי מכון קרולינסקה, ראוס הראה כבר לפני יותר מ-60 שנה שנגיפים יכולים לגרום לגידולים, במחקרי סרקומה בתרנגולות.
claims.quote: a sarcoma in the domestic fowl was transmissible to other fowl

claims.quote: he returned to MIT as a member of its biology faculty, where he remained until 1990

claims.text: לפי ה-Jewish Journal ב-2005, הוא ראה עצמו יהודי חילוני, שהשקפתו והישגיו נטועים בחינוכו היהודי המוקדם.
claims.quote: sees himself now as a secular Jew

claims.text: תומאס רוזנבאום, שהיה אז נשיא קלטק, אמר שתרומתו של בולטימור כנגיפאי שינתה את הביולוגיה והרפואה.
